## Machine shop quote template

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machine-shop-quote-template

Guide

## Machine shop quote template

What a CNC or fabrication quote needs on it, what to keep off it, the terms to decide
once, a filled-in example and a free template to download. The buyer reads a quote to compare it with
two others and to write a purchase order from it; every field below serves one of those.

Download the template (CSV)

### What goes on a machine shop quote

FieldWhy it is there

Your shop's name, address, phone and emailSo the buyer can reach the person who quoted, and a purchase order goes to the right place.Quote number and revisionOne number per quote, and a revision label when you re-quote, so a PO names exactly which prices it accepts.Date and valid-until dateMaterial and machine time get repriced; a quote without an end date can be held against you a year later.Customer company, contact and their RFQ numberBuyers send many RFQs; their reference is how they match your quote to theirs.Part number and drawing revision for every lineThe price is for that revision. When the drawing changes, the revision on your quote shows which one you priced.Description: material, finish and anything else priced inThe buyer compares quotes line by line; saying “6061-T6, clear anodize, certs included” stops a cheaper quote that left them out looking like the same thing.Every quantity asked for, with unit and extended priceSetup and lot minimums spread differently at each quantity, so each break gets its own price, not one price each.Lead time, counted from the order“3 weeks after receipt of order” holds; a calendar date goes stale while the buyer decides.Notes: assumptions and exceptionsAnything you assumed (a tolerance, a material substitute, an inspection level) written down before the PO, not argued about after.TermsPayment, shipping, overruns and the rest, decided once and printed on every quote (list below).

### What stays off it

Your cost basis. The customer sees a price for each part at each quantity; your hourly rates, setup
and cycle minutes, material cost and markup stay in your own records. A quote that shows them invites
the buyer to negotiate each one, and tells a competitor your rates. Keep the basis with the quote on
your side, so you can answer when a reorder is priced differently
(how a machining price is built).

### A filled-in example

The shop, customer, part, dates and prices are made up. The prices are the worked
example in how to quote a CNC
machining job, priced at three quantities.

Example Precision Machining: quote Q-1001, dated 2026-11-27, valid until
2026-12-27. Prepared for Example Customer Co., A. Buyer, purchasing. Lead time: 3 weeks after receipt of order.
PartQtyUnit priceExtended

BRK-1001 Rev BMounting bracket, per drawing BRK-1001 Rev B. 6061-T6 aluminum, clear anodize (outside vendor).1$587.26$587.2610$113.53$1,135.30100$71.65$7,165.00

Notes

- Quoted to drawing BRK-1001 Rev B dated 2026-11-20. A later revision is a new quote.
- Material certifications included. First-article inspection report included on the first lot.
- Customer RFQ 2291.

What to check on the RFQ before you price it, so the notes catch every assumption:
the RFQ review checklist.

### Terms to decide once

Each of these is a question your terms should answer. Decide them for your shop, put them in one
paragraph and print it on every quote. They are prompts, not wording to copy: have your own terms
and conditions reviewed by someone qualified where you do business.

- Validity. How many days the prices hold, and what happens after: a re-quote, or prices adjusted for material.
- Payment. Net 30 or another term, a deposit on large or first orders, and whether you take cards.
- Drawing revision. That the price is for the revision quoted, and a change to the drawing is a new quote or a change order.
- Overruns and underruns. Whether you may ship a few parts over or under the order quantity, and how those are billed.
- Inspection and paperwork. Which certifications, first-article or CMM reports are included, and which are charged extra.
- Shipping. Where ownership and risk pass (FOB your dock or theirs, or an Incoterm), and who pays freight.
- Customer-supplied material. Who carries the cost when material or parts the customer supplied scrap through no fault of yours.
- Changes and cancellation. What the customer owes for material bought and work done when an order is changed or cancelled.
- Export-controlled drawings. Whether you accept ITAR or EAR technical data, and how the customer must mark and send it.

### The template

machine-shop-quote-template.csv opens in Excel,
Google Sheets or LibreOffice. It has the columns Line, Part number, Drawing revision, Description, Material, Finish, Quantity, Unit price, Extended price, Lead time, Notes: one row per quantity
break, so a part quoted at three quantities takes three rows with the same line number. The example
rows are marked; delete them. It holds plain values, no formulas: work out the extended price as
quantity × unit price, and put your shop's header, the customer, the dates and your terms above the
table when you print it.

A spreadsheet works for a few quotes a week. It stops working when you need to find what you quoted
a part at last time, re-quote a revision, see which quotes are about to expire or remember to follow up.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote builds this quote as a PDF from your rate card: your shop's name, logo and contact
lines, a quote number with revisions (“Q-1001 Rev 2, replaces Q-1001”), the date, a valid-until
date from your default number of days, the customer, a lead time from your default, every part with its
revision and description, a row per quantity break with unit and extended prices, the quote's notes and
your terms, saved once in the rate card. It never prints your rates, times or markup. The estimator
checks and sends it; the customer gets a link to accept or decline, and the app reminds you about
follow-ups and quotes about to expire. You can
see how a quote is built.

This page describes common practice for job-shop quotes. It is not legal, tax or
financial advice, and the example's names, dates and prices are made up. Check every quote before you
send it.

## RFQ review checklist

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/rfq-review-checklist

Guide

## RFQ review checklist for machine shops

21 things to check on a request for quote before you price it: the
documents, the part, the quantities and dates, the paperwork and the terms. Most costly quoting
mistakes are not arithmetic; they are a revision, a callout or a clause nobody read. A free checklist to
download and fill in per RFQ is at the end.

Download the checklist (CSV)

### Why review an RFQ before quoting it

A quote is an offer: once the buyer sends a purchase order against it, you have agreed to make that
revision, in that material, to those callouts, by that date, at that price. Reviewing the request first
is where you find what the price must cover and whether you can deliver it at all. ISO 9001:2015 and
AS9100D both ask for this step under clause 8.2.3, “review of the requirements for products and
services”, before a shop commits to supply. This list is a practical start for that review; it does not
by itself meet either standard, and your own quality manual decides what your review records.

In short: documents, the part,
quantity and timing, quality and
paperwork, commercial terms and restrictions.

### The documents

CheckAskWhy it matters

Every part has a drawing or modelDoes each line on the RFQ have a drawing, a model or both, and do the part numbers on them match the RFQ?A line quoted from a description alone is a guess; a drawing that carries another part number means one part was never sent.Drawing revisionWhich revision is each drawing, does it match the revision the RFQ asks for, and is the model the same revision as the drawing?The price is for the revision quoted. A model at Rev C with a drawing at Rev B is two different parts until the buyer says which one governs.Drawing or model governsIf the drawing and the model disagree, which one does the customer say governs, and are there dimensions only on the drawing?Many shops program from the model and inspect to the drawing; a note saying which governs settles the argument before the first article, not after.Referenced specs on handDo you have every specification the drawing calls out (material, finish, heat treat, welding, inspection), at the revision it names?A callout you have not read can add a process, a test or a certification you did not price.

### The part

CheckAskWhy it matters

MaterialIs the material fully specified (alloy, temper or condition, form), can you buy it at the size you need, and is a substitute allowed?“Aluminum” is not a material; 6061-T6 plate and 7075-T651 bar price and machine differently, and an unavailable size changes the blank.Tightest tolerancesWhich features carry the tightest tolerances or GD&T callouts, and can your machines hold and your gauges measure them?One tight bore can decide the machine, the setup count and the inspection time for the whole part.Surface finish and edgesWhat surface roughness is called out, where, and what edge break or deburr note applies?A fine finish on a sealing face may need a finishing pass or a grind; “break all edges” on a part with many edges is real minutes.Threads and holesWhich threads, thread classes and hole depths are called out, and do any need special tools or gauges?Deep holes, small taps and thread gauges you do not own add time and tooling cost.Finish, plating and heat treatWhich outside processes are called out (anodize, plating, passivation, paint, heat treat), to which specification, and who supplies them?Outside processes have lot minimums and lead times of their own, and a masking note can cost more than the coating.Marking and packagingDoes the part need part marking, serial numbers, bagging, special packaging or labels?Small per-part steps add up over a lot and are easy to forget at the quoting stage.

### Quantity and timing

CheckAskWhy it matters

Quantities asked forWhich quantities does the buyer want prices for, is it a one-off, a blanket order or scheduled releases, and is there a prototype lot first?Setup and lot minimums spread differently at each quantity; a blanket order with releases is priced and stocked differently from one lot.Due date against your loadWhen does the buyer need the parts, when must the quote be in, and can you deliver with what is already on the floor?A price you cannot deliver on loses the customer more surely than a high price.Repeat partHave you quoted or made this part number before, at which revision and price, and did that quote win?Last time's price, time and problems are the best estimate you have, and a buyer notices when the same part is priced differently.

### Quality and paperwork

CheckAskWhy it matters

CertificationsDoes the buyer want material certifications, a certificate of conformance or process certs from your finishers?Certs have to be ordered with the material and kept; a mill cert requested after the material arrives may not be available.First-article and inspection reportsIs a first-article inspection required (for aerospace work, often to AS9102), a CMM report, a sampling plan or 100% inspection?A full first-article report on a complex part can take longer than machining the first part, and it is often unpriced.Quality system requirementsDoes the purchase order or the buyer's supplier manual require a quality system registered to ISO 9001 or AS9100, or other quality clauses?Quality clauses on the PO bind you once you accept it; read them at the quote, not when the order arrives.

### Commercial terms and restrictions

CheckAskWhy it matters

Export-controlled technical dataIs the drawing marked ITAR or EAR, or as Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), and can your shop lawfully receive and store it?Export-controlled and CUI drawings have handling rules of their own; ask someone qualified before you open them, not after.Defense and government flowdownsIs it a defense or government job, and which clauses flow down to you (for example DFARS 252.204-7012 on safeguarding covered defense information, or 252.225-7009 on specialty metals)?Flowdowns can restrict where material comes from and how you store the drawings; a clause you cannot meet means no-quote.Customer-supplied materialDoes the customer supply the material or parts, and who pays when one scraps?Free-issue material changes the price and the risk; settle the scrap terms on the quote.Payment and shippingAre the buyer's payment terms and shipping terms (FOB point, who pays freight) ones you accept?Net 90 on a large material buy is a loan to the customer; know it before you price.Quote or no-quoteAfter all of the above: do you want this job at a price the buyer is likely to pay, and if not, have you told them so?A prompt no-quote keeps the buyer's goodwill and your estimator's time for the work you want.

### When the answer is “I don't know”

Ask the buyer before you quote, in one email listing every open question, rather than one question at
a time. Where the buyer will not answer in time, quote with the assumption written in the quote's notes
(“quoted to Rev B; drawing governs; material certs included, first-article report not included”), so
the PO accepts your reading or the buyer corrects it before work starts. The
machine shop quote template has a
notes field for exactly this, and the terms worth deciding once.

### The checklist

rfq-review-checklist.csv opens in Excel,
Google Sheets or LibreOffice: a line at the top for the RFQ, who reviewed it and when, then one row per
check with the columns Section, Check, Question, Why it matters, Answer (yes / no / n/a), Notes. Save one copy per RFQ with the quote. It holds plain
values, no formulas. Drop the rows that never apply to your work and add your own.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote does not replace the review; it puts the facts in front of the estimator and keeps the
record. For 11 of the checks above, the hosted app does this today:

- Every part has a drawing or model. The rule reader matches a drawing to the part whose number it carries and fills that part's blanks from it.
- Drawing revision. Revision is a field on every part and prints on the quote line, so the quote says which revision was priced.
- Material. The reader takes the material line and suggests the matching material from your rate card; a material stated above a parts list applies to every part.
- Tightest tolerances. The reader picks up labelled tolerance lines so the estimator sees them on the review.
- Threads and holes. From a STEP model the app finds the holes and their depths and pre-fills drilling; the estimator ticks which sizes are tapped.
- Finish, plating and heat treat. Finishing and outside services are on the rate card with their per-part price and lot minimum.
- Quantities asked for. The reader takes the quantity lines; every quantity break is priced from the same rate card, with setup and minimums spread at each.
- Due date against your load. The reader takes due dates that carry a year; the Shop load page puts your open jobs on your machines and plans a draft quote's lead time behind them.
- Repeat part. The RFQ review shows “Quoted before: N, M won” for each part before a quote exists, from your own quote history.
- Export-controlled technical data. Job Shop Quote's early access is not set up for CUI or export-controlled drawings; use it only for commercial RFQs.
- Quote or no-quote. Quotes you send are logged as won, lost or expired with the reason, so win rate by customer shows where quoting pays.

Reading is by rules today (AI reading is not switched on yet), and shows each value it took next to the RFQ text it came from, unconfirmed until the estimator confirms the
part. When something a price needs is missing, the quote shows a blocking issue instead of a guess. The
pricing then follows your rate card:
how a machining quote is built.

This page describes common practice for reviewing job-shop RFQs. It is not legal,
export-control, tax or quality-certification advice; the standards and regulations named are for you to
read in their current text. Check every quote before you send it.

## How to calculate material cost for machining

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machining-material-cost

Guide

## How to calculate material cost for a machining quote

Material is the line on a machining quote that is easiest to get roughly right and
easiest to get quietly wrong: a blank sized from the part instead of the stock, a price from last
quarter, a supplier minimum left off a one-piece order. Here is the method, the four ways shops buy
stock, one bracket priced all four ways at 1, 10 and 100, and what the
numbers show.

### The method in five steps

- Size the blank, not the part. Take the part's envelope (its bounding box) and add
stock on every side for facing, clamping and cleanup, then round up to a size you can buy or saw.
Turned parts add a cut-off and facing allowance to the length and take the next bar diameter up.

- Weigh it. Weight = length × width × thickness (or π × r² × length for round bar) ×
density in lb/in³. Take the density from the alloy's datasheet or your supplier; a figure in g/cm³
converts by × 0.0361273 (16.387064 cm³ per in³ ÷ 453.59237 g per lb).

- Price it the way you buy it. Plate cut to size is often priced by weight (per
pound or per hundredweight, 100 lb). Bar, tube and extrusion are priced by length, and either you bill
the length each part uses or, when the rest of the bar has no other job to go to, the whole bars the
order needs. Precut blanks and sheets are priced per piece. Add a share for saw kerf and drop where you
price by weight or by length used.

- Price the parts you start, not the parts you ship. If you expect some parts to
scrap, the order needs more blanks: parts started = parts shipped ÷ (1 − fallout), rounded up.

- Keep the minimum and add your markup. Suppliers have minimum charges and cut
charges; a one-off part still pays them. Then the markup on material: handling, ordering, storage and
the cash tied up until the customer pays.

### A worked example

A 6061 aluminum bracket whose model measures 4 × 3 × 0.5 in,
quoted at 1, 10 and 100 with 3% expected
fallout and a 20% material markup. Every price, allowance and scrap
share here is made up to show the arithmetic; they are not market prices for any metal,
supplier or region. Use your supplier's current prices.

- Blank: 0.0625 in a side on 4 × 3 ×
0.5 in, rounded up to the next 1/8 in, is 4.125 × 3.125 ×
0.625 in: 8.057 in³, and at 0.0975 lb/in³,
0.786 lb.

- Plate: 6061-T6 aluminum plate, 5/8 in, quoted by the supplier at
$525.00 per hundredweight, which is $5.25 a pound, plus
25% for kerf and drop and a $40.00 minimum
charge.

- Flat bar: 5/8 × 3-1/4 in 6061-T6 aluminum flat bar at $14.80
a foot, sold in 12 ft bars ($177.60 a bar). Each part takes
4.125 in plus 0.125 in for the saw and facing, 4.25 in; after
a 2 in end that cannot become a part, one bar gives 33 blanks.

- Precut blank: 6061-T6 precut blank, 5/8 × 3-1/8 × 4-1/8 in, $13.50 a piece,
one part each.

- Starts: at 3% fallout, 1 part needs
2 starts, 10 need 11 and 100 need
104.

Material for the made-up bracket, before markup, for the whole line, and per part shipped (rounded up to the cent). Checked to the cent against Job Shop Quote's costing engine.
Bought as1 (2 started)10 (11 started)100 (104 started)

Plate by the pound ($5.25/lb, 25% scrap, $40.00 minimum)$40.00$40.00 a part$56.70$5.67 a part$536.12$5.37 a partFlat bar by the foot used ($14.80/ft, 10% scrap)$11.53$11.53 a part$63.42$6.35 a part$599.65$6.00 a partFlat bar in whole 12 ft bars (33 parts a bar)$177.60$177.60 a part$177.60$17.76 a part$710.40$7.11 a partPrecut blank ($13.50 each)$27.00$27.00 a part$148.50$14.85 a part$1,404.00$14.04 a part

What the table shows:

- At one part, the minimum is the price. Two plate blanks come to
$10.31 by weight, but the $40.00 minimum is what the
supplier bills, so it is what the quote must carry. Leave it off and a one-piece order loses it.

- Whole bars cost the most on small orders. Buying a 12 ft bar
for 2 blanks puts $177.60 on the quote against
$11.53 for the length used. Which one is right depends on whether the
rest of that bar has another job to go to; if it will sit on the rack, bill the bar.

- At volume, the drop is in the bar count. 104 blanks at
33 a bar need 4 bars, and the last one is only partly used: it has room
for 28 more blanks, about 119 in, billed with
the order.

- Precut blanks cost more per part and save saw time. At 100 they
are $1,404.00 against $536.12 from
plate, a gap that has to be weighed against the sawing, squaring and handling time the plate needs,
which belongs on the routing, not in the material line.

- Markup comes last. At 20%, the 100-part
plate line goes from $536.12 to
$643.34.

### Mistakes that lose money on material

- Pricing from the finished part. The model's volume is what is left after
machining; you buy the blank. On a pocketed part the blank can weigh several times the part.

- An old price. Metal prices move from month to month. A rate card typed in once
quotes last season's metal; date every price and check the old ones before you send.

- Pricing the parts shipped. At 3% fallout, a hundred parts shipped means
a hundred and four blanks bought.

- Dropping the minimum and cut charges. They are small on a big order and most of
the cost on a small one.

- Mixing up the two kinds of scrap. Kerf and drop are material lost from each
blank; fallout is whole parts lost. Count each once.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Put each material on the rate card once, the way you buy it: by weight (a price per pound or per
hundredweight, kept exactly as the supplier quotes it, with the density and a scrap share), by length (a
price per foot or per metre, the cut allowance and, if you buy fixed bars, the bar length and remnant,
so a line is charged the whole bars it needs), or by the stock piece with how many parts it yields; each
with its minimum charge. When an RFQ comes with a STEP model, Job Shop Quote suggests the blank from the
part's bounding box as above, and you can change it. Each line is priced on the parts started at the
line's fallout, with the material markup from your rate card, and a material with no price or no blank
size blocks the line instead of pricing it as free. Every price keeps the date it was set, and a draft
quote warns when it prices from one older than your limit; see
material price tracking. The
charges in the table are the ones the app gives for the same inputs, checked by a test in its code.

For the rest of the price (setups, cycle time, outside processes and quantity breaks), see
how to quote a CNC machining job
and how to estimate CNC
machining time.

This page explains a common estimating method. It is not engineering, accounting
or financial advice, it does not quote metal prices, and the figures in it are made up. Check every
quote before you send it.

## How to price a rush job

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-to-price-a-rush-job

Guide

## How to price a rush job in a machine shop

A rush costs the shop real money: overtime, the job it pushes aside, material and
outside processing bought fast. A flat expedite fee guesses at that. Here is how to cost a rush the
way you cost any job, a worked example at 1, 10 and 100
parts, and why one percentage cannot be right at every quantity.

### What a rush actually costs

- Hours at a higher rate. Work done on overtime, a second shift or a weekend
costs the operator's premium and the payroll costs on it. Price those hours at a second rate for
the same machine, not by stretching the cycle time.

- The job it bumps. If another customer's job is set up on the machine you
need, pulling it off means tearing it down now and setting it up again later. That setup is paid
twice, and the rush is what causes it.

- Material bought fast. Same-day or next-day delivery, a cut-to-size charge
from a distributor's counter, or a price above your usual supplier's for stock that is on a shelf
today.

- Outside processing expedited. Platers, anodizers, heat treaters and coaters
often run an expedited service at a higher price or a higher lot minimum. Ask them; their quote
is the number to use.

- Inspection and paperwork on the same clock. A first article, certs or a
customer's source inspection still have to happen, now inside the shorter window.

- The promises you move. Other jobs ship later. That is not a line on this
quote, but it is a reason to decide whether to take the rush at all, and what lead time you can
actually promise without breaking the others.

### A worked example

The mounting bracket from the CNC
quoting guide, quoted at its normal lead time there, and here again as a rush.
Every number is made up to show the arithmetic; none is a typical overtime premium,
expedite price or surcharge for any region or trade. Use your own.

- Overtime: “Op 1: face, profile, pockets”, “Op 2: flip, face to thickness, drill and tap”, “Deburr and inspect” run on overtime, at the mill's
$123.85 an hour plus a $24.00 premium =
$147.85 an hour. Programming and the first-article check stay on the normal shift
at $123.85.

- The bumped job: 50 min to tear down the job that was on the
mill and set it up again later, at the normal rate: $103.21, once per order.

- Material: the same plate and price per pound, plus
$85.00 for same-day delivery, once per order.

- Clear anodize, 2-day expedite (outside vendor): $5.25 a part, minimum
$300.00 a lot (the normal service in the CNC guide is cheaper).

- Markups: as in the CNC guide; the delivery charge is a purchased item, so it
takes the material markup.

The made-up bracket, normal and rush, at three quantities. Each component is rounded to the cent, then summed; the price each is rounded up to the cent.
Line1 part10 parts100 parts

Normal lead time: line total$587.26$1,135.30$7,165.00Rush: setups (incl. the bumped job)$411.88$411.88$411.88Rush: run time$128.14$704.75$6,663.11Rush: anodize, expedited$300.00$300.00$546.00Rush: same-day plate delivery$85.00$85.00$85.00Rush: line total$1,011.52$1,653.10$8,687.00What the rush adds$424.26 (72.2%)$517.80 (45.6%)$1,522.00 (21.2%)Normal + flat 25%$734.08$1,419.13$8,956.25Flat surcharge vs the costed rush$277.44 short$233.97 short$269.25 over

What the table shows:

- The rush adds a different share at every quantity. Costed line by line it
adds 72.2% at 1 part, 45.6% at
10 parts and 21.2% at 100 parts. The bumped
setup, the delivery and the anodizer's higher minimum are fixed per order, so they weigh most on a
small lot; the overtime premium grows with the hours, so it is most of the rush on a large one.

- A flat 25% is wrong both ways. It comes up
$277.44 short at 1 part and $233.97 short at 10 parts, and charges $269.25 more than the rush costs at 100 parts. Short means the shop pays for the customer's deadline; over means the shop is easier to beat
on the next rush.

- If you want a margin for the disruption, add it on purpose. Cost the rush,
then add a premium you choose for the promises it moves. Then you know what the premium is and
what is just cost.

### Before you say yes

- Check the machines, not your memory. Which jobs are on the machines this
operation needs, and when do they finish? A rush that only fits by making two other jobs late is
a decision, not a quote.

- Call the outside vendors first. An anodizer or heat treater who cannot do it
in time sets the lead time, whatever your own shop can do.

- Quote the rush and the normal lead time side by side. Two lines, two dates,
two prices. The customer picks, and the rush price reads as a choice, not a penalty.

- Write the date as a condition. "Ships N working days after the order and the
approved drawing" protects the date from a purchase order that arrives two days late.

- Keep the rush in its own lines. Priced as separate lines, or as its own
revision of the quote, the rush can be taken off again: when the same part comes back on a normal
lead time, it is the normal price that gets reused, not last time's expedite.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Job Shop Quote has no rush switch: a rush is priced like any other line, with the rush costs typed
in. Add the overtime rate as a second machine on your rate card ("3-axis mill (overtime)"),
put the operations that run on overtime on it, add the bumped job as an operation with setup only,
the expedited service as its own finishing operation with its lot minimum, and the delivery as an
extra per order. Every quantity break then follows, each figure showing the rate it came from. The
example above is priced to the cent the app gives for the same inputs, checked by a test in its code.
To see whether a date needs a rush at all, the app's
shop load and lead time page
places your open jobs on the machines and gives each quantity break a lead time behind them. Revise a
sent quote to offer the rush as a second version.

The rest of the price: how to
quote a CNC machining job, how
to work out a machine shop hourly rate, and what goes on the quote you send, the
machine shop quote template.

This page explains a common costing method. It is not accounting, tax, legal or
financial advice, it does not say what overtime pay the law requires, and the rates, premiums,
prices and times in it are made up. Check every quote before you send it.

### Quote your next rush with every cost on it

## How to quote first article inspection

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/how-to-quote-first-article-inspection

Guide

## How to quote first article inspection (AS9102)

An aerospace PO that calls for a first article inspection report asks for hours of
work that never touch a machine: ballooning the drawing, measuring every characteristic on the first
part and filling in the forms. On a small order that work can cost more than the machining, and it is
the line shops most often leave off. Here is what the work is, when a partial first article is due,
and one part priced with and without it at 1, 10 and
100.

### What a first article is, and what it is not

AS9102 is the aerospace standard for first article inspection (FAI): a documented check, on a part
from the first production run, that every design characteristic on the drawing and every requirement
on the PO was met. It is recorded on three forms:

- Form 1, part number accountability: the part, its drawing and revision, and any
sub-assemblies.

- Form 2, product accountability: the raw material, the specifications, the special
processes (plating, anodizing, heat treat and the like) and any functional tests, each with the
certificate that proves it.

- Form 3, characteristic accountability: every dimension, tolerance and note on
the drawing, numbered (ballooned) on the drawing and listed with its measured result.

A first-piece check is not a first article. Measuring the critical features of the first part off
the machine before running the rest is part of the setup, and the
CNC quoting guide prices it as
such (60 minutes on the mill). An AS9102 report is a separate job with a
separate deliverable, and it stays on the routing in every variant below. Which revision of AS9102
applies, and whether the customer accepts their own form or software output, is set by the PO and
its quality clauses: read them before you price.

### What the work takes

- Balloon the drawing. Number every characteristic: each dimension, tolerance,
thread, surface finish, note and flag note. A busy drawing can carry well over a hundred.

- Plan the inspection. Decide which gauge or CMM program checks each one; a CMM
program written for the first article is time too.

- Measure the first part. Every characteristic, with the result written down, not
just a pass.

- Collect the certificates. Mill certs for the material and a certificate from
every special-process vendor, some of whom charge for one.

- Fill in the forms and file them. And answer the customer's questions when their
quality team reviews the package.

None of that scales with quantity: it is the same for one part as for a thousand, so it belongs in
the quote as a charge per line or per order, not per part.

### A worked example

The anodized 6061 mounting bracket from the CNC quoting guide, now for a customer whose PO calls for
an AS9102 first article. Inspection time is charged at $95.00 an hour (a CMM and bench rate of its
own, lower than the mill's $123.85). Every time, rate and price here is
made up to show the arithmetic; none of it is a benchmark for what a first article takes or
costs, and AS9102 sets no price.

- Full AS9102 first article: balloon the drawing and plan the inspection (45 min), measure every characteristic on the first part (90 min), fill in Forms 1 to 3 and collect the certs (60 min), plus the anodizer's certificate for Form 2 ($25.00): 195 minutes, $333.75 before markup.
- Partial (delta) first article after a revision: re-balloon the changed characteristics (15 min), measure the changed characteristics (30 min), update Forms 1 to 3 (30 min): 75 minutes, $118.75 before markup.

The made-up bracket's price per part and for the line, by first-article variant. Checked to the cent against Job Shop Quote's costing engine.
Variant110100

No first-article report$587.26 each$587.26 for the line$113.53 each$1,135.30 for the line$71.65 each$7,165.00 for the lineFull AS9102 first article$924.76 each$924.76 for the line$147.28 each$1,472.80 for the line$75.03 each$7,503.00 for the linePartial (delta) first article after a revision$706.01 each$706.01 for the line$125.40 each$1,254.00 for the line$72.84 each$7,284.00 for the line

What the table shows:

- On one part, the first article is 36% of the price. The full report adds
$337.50 to a $587.26 part
($333.75 of inspection and certificate, and $3.75 of markup
on the certificate). Quote it without that line and the shop does that work for nothing.

- Spread over the order, it fades. At 10 parts it adds
$33.75 a part; at 100, $3.38. The
charge is the same; only the share each part carries changes.

- A partial first article is a smaller charge, not none. After a revision that
changes a few characteristics, re-ballooning and measuring only those, and updating the forms, adds
$118.75 to the line here, against $337.50 for a
full one.

### When a new or partial first article is due

Once a part has a complete first article, repeat orders do not need another, until something
changes. The events AS9102 lists include a change to the design that affects the part's
characteristics, a change in the manufacturing source, process, inspection method, location,
tooling or materials, and a lapse in production (two years in the standard). The customer can ask for
more. A partial ("delta") first article covers only what the change affected. So check, on every repeat
RFQ: has the revision changed, has anything about how you make it changed, and when did you last ship
it? Your own records answer the last two; the drawing answers the first.

### How to put it on the quote

- Price it as time, at an inspection rate. Minutes on the inspection bench or the
CMM, charged once per line, the same way you charge a setup.

- Say it on the quote. "Includes AS9102 first article report" or "first article
report not included" in the notes settles the question before the PO arrives, not after. When a
customer wants it priced separately, give it a line of its own at quantity one.

- Carry the vendors' certificate charges. They are small and easy to forget.

- Do not charge it again on a repeat order that does not need it, and do not
forget the partial one when the revision changes.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

Add your inspection bench or CMM to the rate card as a machine with its own rate. On a quote line,
add the first article as operations on that machine with setup minutes and a cycle time of zero (the
app accepts zero for setup-only work such as programming or a first article), and a certificate
charge as an extra with a lot amount. The app then charges it once for the line, spreads it across
each quantity break, and prints the per-part prices. The prices in the table are the ones the app gives
for the same inputs, checked by a test in its code. Once the RFQ's drawing PDF is in, the RFQ page
also has a "First article list" download: a draft of Form 3's characteristic list read from the
drawing's text (toleranced dimensions with their limits, geometric tolerances, threads, finishes,
numbered notes, material and finish), numbered so the numbers can be the balloon numbers. It is a
draft to check against the drawing: a dimension with no text on the PDF, or a scanned drawing,
is not in it. Job Shop Quote does not fill in Forms 1 and 2, draw the balloons or record results. The
RFQ review checklist has the question
to ask before you price: is a first article required, and to which standard?

This page explains a common estimating approach and summarises a published
standard in plain words. It is not quality, legal or engineering advice, it is not a substitute for
the standard or your customer's requirements, and the figures in it are made up. Check every quote
before you send it.

## How tolerances change a machining quote

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machining-tolerances

Guide

## How tolerances change a machining quote

Two drawings of the same part can cost very different amounts to make, and the
difference is often one callout: a bore at ±.005 is a drill and a pass, the same bore at ±.0005 can be
a reamer, a slower finish, a gauge and a check on every part. Here is how to read a tolerance as a
zone, the four bands estimators sort them into, what ISO 2768 and fits like H7 mean in inches, and
where the cost goes on the quote.

### Read a tolerance as a zone

A tolerance is the room a dimension has to vary. What decides how hard it is to hold is the full
width of that room, the tolerance zone, not how it is written. ±.001 is a zone of
.002 in; +.002/-.000 is a zone of .002 in too, with all of it on one side. A tight one-sided tolerance
can be as hard as a looser-looking bilateral one, so convert every callout to its zone before you
compare them. On a drawing, the tightest zone usually sets the process, the machine and the inspection
for the whole part.

### Four bands, and what each asks of the shop

Estimators sort tolerances into rough bands. The limits below are shop-floor rules of thumb, not a
standard: what counts as tight depends on the material, the feature, its size and your machines. They
are the defaults Job Shop Quote's tolerance check uses.

Tolerance bands by zone, in inches. Rules of thumb, not a standard.
BandToleranceWhat it usually asks

Standard±.005 in and looser (a zone of .010 in or more)Ordinary roughing and finishing on a CNC mill or lathe, checked with calipers.Close±.001 up to ±.005 in (a zone of .002 to under .010 in)A finish pass and a micrometer or bore gauge on the feature; most CNC machines hold it.Tight±.0005 up to ±.001 in (a zone of .001 to under .002 in)Finish passes at a lighter cut, tool wear watched, in-process gauging, and more parts checked per lot.Precisiontighter than ±.0005 in (a zone under .001 in)Often grinding, honing or reaming to size, a temperature-stable check and a CMM or air gauge; some shops send it out.

### Callouts as they arrive, read as zones

RFQs bring tolerances in every form: thousandths in an email, millimetres with a comma decimal from
a European customer, a general tolerance class in the title block, a fit symbol on a bore. Each row
below is read by the same code that reads an RFQ in Job Shop Quote, and a test in the app checks that
this table matches what it shows.

Each callout's full zone in inches and millimetres, and its band. * The zone depends on the feature's size; shown for the size named.
CalloutMeansZoneBand

+/- .005Five thousandths either way0.0100 in0.254 mmStandard±.002Two thousandths either way0.0040 in0.102 mmClose+.002/-.000Up to two thousandths over, nothing under (one-sided)0.0020 in0.051 mmClose±.0005Half a thousandth either way0.0010 in0.025 mmTight+.0005/-.0000Half a thousandth over, nothing under0.00050 in0.013 mmPrecision±0,02 mmTwo hundredths of a millimetre either way (a comma decimal)0.0016 in0.040 mmTightISO 2768-mThe general tolerance class 'medium': ±0.2 mm on a 6 to 30 mm dimension0.0157 in0.400 mm *StandardISO 2768-fThe general tolerance class 'fine': ±0.1 mm on a 6 to 30 mm dimension0.0079 in0.200 mm *CloseH7An ISO 286 hole fit, grade IT7: a 21 µm zone on an 18 to 30 mm bore0.00083 in0.021 mm *Precision

### ISO 2768: the general tolerance in the title block

A drawing that says "ISO 2768-m" (often with a second letter, K, H or L, for the geometric
tolerances) sets the tolerance of every dimension that has none of its own. The value grows with the
size of the dimension. The linear values from ISO 2768-1, in millimetres either way:

ISO 2768-1 general tolerances for linear dimensions, ± mm, by nominal size in mm. Larger sizes are in the standard.
Classover 0.5–3over 3–6over 6–30over 30–120over 120–400

f (fine)±0.05±0.05±0.1±0.15±0.2m (medium)±0.1±0.1±0.2±0.3±0.5c (coarse)±0.2±0.3±0.5±0.8±1.2v (very coarse)—±0.5±1±1.5±2.5

The first column starts at 0.5 mm and the others start just above the size named, so "over 6–30"
means over 6 up to 30 mm. A general class rarely sets the price on its own: "fine" on a 20 mm dimension
is ±0.1 mm, about ±.004 in, a close tolerance most CNC work holds. The dimensions toleranced on their
own are the ones to look for.

### Fits: H7, g6 and the rest

A letter and number on a bore or a pin (H7, h6, H7/g6) is an ISO 286 fit. The letter places the
zone relative to the nominal size; the number is the IT grade, which sets its width, and that width
grows with the size. On an 18 to 30 mm feature, IT6 is 13 µm (about .0005 in) and IT7 is 21 µm
(about .0008 in): an H7 bore of that size is a precision feature by the bands above, which is why it
usually means a reamer or a boring bar and a bore gauge, not a drill. Look up the size you have in
the standard's tables before you quote it.

### Where the cost goes on the quote

Tolerance has no price of its own. It costs money through the work it adds, and that work belongs
on the quote line where you can see it:

- Run time. Finish passes at a lighter cut, a slower feed, a spring pass, tool
changes to keep wear in check. Add the minutes to the operation's cycle time; the
machining time guide
shows how cycle time builds up.

- An extra operation. Reaming, honing or grinding to size is an operation of its
own, in house or as an
outside process.

- Inspection. A gauge you need to buy or calibrate, a CMM program, checking every
part instead of a sample. Inspection time is setup minutes on an inspection machine, charged once
per line, the same way the
first article guide
prices it.

- Fallout. The tighter the zone, the more parts land outside it. Start more parts
than the order: a fallout percentage on the line does this.

- Or a question. A tolerance tighter than the part's function needs is common.
Asking the customer whether ±.0005 on a clearance hole could be ±.002 can be worth more than
pricing it.

### Doing it in Job Shop Quote

The RFQ review reads the tolerance text from the customer's email or drawing (the AI reader keeps it
exactly as written) and, when the tightest tolerance is tighter than ±.005 in, names it with its zone
and band and says what to check: "Precision: +.0005/-.0000, a 0.00050 in (0.013 mm) zone." It reads
±, +/-, one-sided limits, inches and millimetres (comma decimals too), ISO 2768 classes and ISO 286 fits,
and skips angles. It never changes a price: the minutes, operations and fallout above are yours to
add, and the quote is priced from your rate card. Fits and ISO 2768 classes are read at a typical size
(the note says which), because the RFQ does not say how big the feature is. The
RFQ review checklist has the
tolerance questions to ask before you price.

This page explains common estimating practice and summarises published
standards in plain words. It is not engineering advice and not a substitute for ISO 2768, ISO 286 or
your customer's drawing. The band limits are rules of thumb. Check every quote before you send it.

## FAQ

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/faq

FAQ

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I use Job Shop Quote today?

Yes. Sign up free at https://jobshop-quote.marisstella.app/sign-up. The Early access plan covers up to 40 RFQs a month for 3 people, with no card. It prices the parts you enter, and what it measures from STEP, IGES, STL and DXF files, from your rate card, builds the quote PDF, emails it when your estimator sends it, and keeps the won/lost log. Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet. Until it is, the app reads them by fixed rules: labelled lines (Part number, Qty, Material, Finish, Due) and parts tables with a header row, each value shown with the line it came from. You check those and enter the rest yourself.

### Does the AI decide my prices?

No. Prices come only from the rates, minimums and markups you set. The AI reads the RFQ and drawings and proposes setups and cycle times with its reasoning shown; your estimator accepts or corrects them, and the dollar math is plain arithmetic on your rate table.

### How does it price material: by weight, by the bar or by the foot?

Whichever way you buy it. Each material on your rate table is priced by weight (your price per lb or per cwt and density, plus scrap), by the stock piece (a sheet or a cut blank), or by length for bar, tube and extrusion: your price per foot or per metre, a cut allowance for kerf and facing, and, if you buy in fixed bars, the bar length and remnant, so a line is charged the whole bars its parts need. You can import these from your supplier's price list as a spreadsheet: before you save, each row shows its price change and the open quotes priced at the old price, and the supplier and the list's date are kept in each price's history. A price per cwt or per metre is kept exactly as your supplier quotes it, so $412.50/cwt prices at $4.125/lb, not a rounded $4.13.

### What does it read?

The STEP, IGES, STL and DXF measurements work today; reading email text and PDF drawings with AI is not switched on in the hosted app yet. RFQ email text and PDF drawings, including scans, plus STEP and DXF files. A STEP solid gives the blank size and, with your machine's measured removal rate, a roughing time; with your seconds per hole and, if you enter one, your drill feed for each hole's depth, a drilling time that counts a counterbored hole once, flags holes deeper than 3× their diameter and leaves bores over 1 in to you; tick which hole sizes are threaded and, with your seconds per tapped hole, it adds a tapping time. A DXF flat pattern gives a laser, waterjet or plasma cutting time from its cut length and pierces at your cut speed (one per machine, or your own speed for each material and thickness from your cut charts), and a press-brake time from its bend lines; on a material sold by the sheet, with your sheet size and nest gap, it counts how many flat blanks fit on one sheet (a rectangular nest, so a nesting program may fit more, never fewer). An IGES solid gives the blank size and hole locations like a STEP file (no volume: send STEP for that). An STL mesh gives its size and, when closed, its volume; an STL carries no units, so your estimator picks millimetres or inches. Native SolidWorks files are not measured yet.

### What happens when a drawing is unclear?

The value is flagged for your estimator with the drawing page it came from. It is never filled in with a guess.

### Will it send quotes to my customers?

No. Your estimator reviews and approves every quote and sends it themselves: by email from the app, as a PDF, or copied into your own email or ERP.

### Will you use my drawings to train AI models?

No. Your drawings, rates and quotes are used only to quote for your shop. They are never used to train AI models and never shared with another shop.

### Can I send CUI or export-controlled (ITAR/EAR) drawings?

Not during early access: it isn't set up for controlled data. Use it only for commercial RFQs. The page for CMMC-conscious shops explains why.

### Does it connect to my ERP or quoting system?

Not yet in the hosted app: download the quote PDF or copy it across. A QuickBooks Online connection, which turns a won quote into an invoice, is built and switches on once Intuit approves it. Tell us which system you use at hello@marisstella.app; that decides what gets connected next.

### What does it cost?

The Early access plan is free, with no card. Paid plans start at $199 a month, priced from what it costs to run; they are not on sale yet. Nobody is moved onto a paid plan without choosing it.

### Who is building it?

Maris Stella Labs LLC, a small software company that also makes Grant Autopilot for nonprofits.

Something else? Email hello@marisstella.app.

### Try it on your own RFQs

The Early access plan is free and needs no card.

## CNC quoting software that prices from your own rate card

For the owner or estimator who quotes machined parts today in a spreadsheet or from memory. You enter your machines, materials and outside processes once; each quote line is then priced by plain arithmetic on those rates, with every figure showing the rate it used.

Start free

### What it does

- A rate card of machines (hourly rate, optional setup rate, default setup), materials (per lb with density and scrap, per stock piece or by the foot, with a minimum charge), finishing and outside services (per part with a lot minimum), markups on labor, material and outside work, and a line minimum
- Each line priced at every quantity break from setup, cycle time, material and finishing, with the rates frozen into the quote so later rate changes never move a sent price
- Blocking issues instead of guesses: a line missing a cycle time, a material price or a blank size says so and is not priced
- Import the rate card from your own spreadsheet (.xlsx or CSV, read in the browser), and download it again as one Excel workbook with a tab per kind
- A quote PDF on your letterhead with your logo, showing prices, dates, lead time and terms and none of the costs, rates or markups behind them
- Revisions (Q-1001 Rev 2) with what changed from the last one, side by side, and an optional "Changes from" section on the customer PDF
- A default fallout percentage, so 100 good parts at 3% start 104 without typing it on each line

- Reading RFQ emails and PDF drawings with AI is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet; until it is, labelled lines and parts tables are read by fixed rules and you enter the rest
- Setup and cycle times are yours to enter, or suggested from STEP and DXF measurements at the rates you set; nothing is assumed
- No ERP connection is on yet; the quote is a PDF you download or email

## Sheet metal quoting from the DXF flat pattern

For fabrication shops that quote laser-cut, waterjet or plasma parts and press-brake work. Upload the customer's DXF and the quote line starts with the cut, pierce and bend times at your own speeds, and the sheets the order needs from a nest of the flat pattern.

Start free

### What it does

- Cut length, pierces and bend lines measured from an ASCII DXF flat pattern, each with a confidence and flag shown on the RFQ
- "Cut from DXF" and "Bend from DXF" operations pre-filled at the machine's cut speed, pierce seconds and seconds per bend
- Cut speeds per material and thickness from your own cut chart, typed in or imported from a CSV, so a 0.5 in A36 part is timed at that gauge's speed
- The blank from the flat size and the material row's sheet thickness, and parts per sheet from a rectangular nest on the row's sheet width, length and gap
- The same rate card, quantity breaks, finishing and quote PDF as machined parts

### What it does not do yet

- Nesting is rectangular: L-shapes and other odd outlines are not nested by their true shape yet
- A DXF whose outline or holes read with low confidence, or whose bend lines are only dashed, gets no suggestion; you enter the times
- No cut speeds are assumed: with none on your card for the material, the machine's default speed applies, and with none at all nothing is suggested

## Quote from the customer's STEP file

For machine shops that get 3D models with their RFQs. The app measures the solid and turns what it finds into suggested operations at the rates you set, each labelled with how it was worked out, for the estimator to accept or change.

Start free

### What it does

- STEP solids measured for size, volume and holes; IGES solids for size and holes; STL meshes for size and volume
- The solid's bounding box pre-fills the blank, and with one machine that has a measured removal rate, a "Rough from CAD" operation
- Hole locations pre-fill "Drill from CAD" at the machine's seconds per hole plus each hole's depth at its drill feed, with counterbores counted once and bores over 1 in left out
- Drill feeds by material, and peck time for holes deeper than 3×D at the machine's peck depth and seconds per peck
- Tapping: the estimator ticks which hole sizes are threaded and the quote adds "Tap from CAD" at the machine's seconds per tapped hole

### What it does not do yet

- Native SolidWorks and other proprietary CAD files are stored but not measured
- One time per tapped hole: tap size and pitch are not timed separately yet
- Only roughing, drilling, tapping and pecking are timed from the model; enter the other operations' times yourself

## Repeat parts quoted from what you quoted before

Most job shops quote the same part numbers again and again. The app shows what you quoted a part at before, what won and what lost, and lets you start the new quote from the last won one, priced from today's rate card.

Start free

### What it does

- "Quoted before: N earlier quotes" on each line and on the RFQ review: quote number, customer, date, status, PO or loss reason, revision, unit price at each break, material and operations
- "Use these inputs" copies an earlier line's cost inputs onto a draft and re-prices it from today's rates
- An optional shop setting pre-fills each new line whose part number and revision match a won quote, labelled "Pre-filled from Q-1001"
- Routings: save a line's operations and finishing as a named routing with a part family, apply or append it on any line, edit it on its own page
- Up to three routings suggested from the line's material and description, each with the evidence it rests on from your own earlier lines

### What it does not do yet

- Routings hold operations and times, never prices: a routing always prices at today's rate card
- Suggestions come only from your shop's own records, so a new shop has none until it has quoted

In the app today

## Material prices with dates, history and the quotes they change

Metal prices move, and a quote priced off a stale number loses money or loses the job. The app dates every price on your rate card, keeps its history, and shows which open quotes were priced at a price the card no longer has.

Start free

### What it does

- "Price set N days ago" on each material, amber past the shop's limit (90 days by default), and a flag on draft lines that use a stale price
- A price history per material: who set it, when, by how much it moved, and from which supplier's price list and date
- A supplier's price sheet imported from a spreadsheet, with a preview of each price move and the open quotes it touches before anything is saved
- "Quotes this changes": every open quote priced at a price the card no longer has, filtered by how far it moved
- Bar, tube and extrusion priced by the foot, with cut allowance, bar length and remnant, charged in whole bars; prices per cwt and per metre kept exactly

### What it does not do yet

- Nothing re-prices on its own: drafts are re-priced when the estimator presses Re-price, and sent quotes keep the price the customer saw
- Prices come from your rate card and your suppliers' sheets; there is no live metal price feed

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to quote CNC turning and lathe parts
- How to quote sheet metal and laser cut parts
- Machine shop markup and margin

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Can I load my supplier's price list?

Yes, as a spreadsheet: the Materials import reads price per lb, per piece, per foot, per cwt or per metre, keeps the supplier and the list's date in each price's history, and shows the moves before you save.

## Online quote acceptance

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/online-quote-acceptance

In the app today

## Quotes your customer can accept online, with a PO number

Once the estimator marks a quote sent, the app emails the exact PDF and can add a link where the customer accepts or declines without an account. An acceptance marks the quote won at the quantity they chose; a decline marks it lost with their reason.

Start free

### What it does

- "Email to customer" sends the PDF frozen at sending (checked against its SHA-256), From your shop, Reply-To the estimator, with the shop's signature
- The customer's link shows the quote as sent and the PDF, never rates, costs or markups; they pick one quoted quantity per part, type a name and an optional PO number and note
- Accepting marks the quote won at the chosen breaks' total with the PO; declining marks it lost with "Declined online" and the reason
- The estimators who made or emailed the quote get the answer by email; links can be turned off at once

### What it does not do yet

- One answer per quote; a quantity the quote does not carry needs a new quote
- No e-signature line on acceptance yet
- The app never sends a quote by itself: an estimator presses send

### Free guides on this

- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)
- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to set quantity price breaks

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does my customer need an account?

No. The link opens the quote as it was sent. Only a hash of the link's token is stored, and the link takes no answer past the quote's valid-until day, and stops working when you turn it off.

## Quote follow-up

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/quote-follow-up-software

In the app today

## Follow up on every quote you send

A quote that is never followed up is a quote half lost. Sending a quote sets its first follow-up day; the quote log and a morning email tell each estimator which quotes are due, and every call or email is logged on the quote.

Start free

### What it does

- A first follow-up day set when the quote is sent, a number of days after sending that the shop chooses (3 by default; a weekend moves to Monday)
- A "Follow up" card on the quote log: quotes due today, longest overdue first, with contact, total, sent day, valid-until, estimator and the last note
- "Log follow-up" records what happened and the next day: in 1 to 14 days, a date, or no more follow-ups
- One email each morning to each estimator listing their own quotes due, and another listing quotes that expire today or tomorrow
- Quotes expire the day after their valid-until day, and Revise starts the next revision

### What it does not do yet

- The follow-up itself is yours: the app reminds and logs, it does not email the customer for you
- Each member can turn the reminder emails off for themselves

### Free guides on this

- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)
- Machine shop quoting software compared

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Which quotes come up for follow-up?

Sent quotes whose follow-up day has come. Won, lost, expired and replaced quotes never do, and a quote the expiry email already names is left out of the follow-up email.

## Win/loss tracking

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/quote-win-rate-tracking

In the app today

## Your quote win rate, and where you win and lose

Mark each quote won (with the PO) or lost (with the reason), or let the customer's online answer do it, and the Win/loss page shows where your prices win, where they lose, and at what price.

Start free

### What it does

- Win rate and won value by customer, material, machine and markup band, over 90 days, 12 months or all time
- Win rate by month and by estimator, by the routing a line was built from, and by part family
- The cost-weighted markup of won against lost quotes, and lost reasons tallied
- "What price did we win at": each part's won and lost quotes with every quantity break's unit price
- A CSV download of the report

### What it does not do yet

- Counted from your own decided quotes only; rows under 5 decided quotes are marked "few"
- Expired quotes are shown but not counted in the win rate

### Free guides on this

- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate
- How to quote a CNC machining job

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### How is the win rate counted?

Won divided by won plus lost, from the quotes your shop marked won or lost (or the customer answered online). Expired quotes are listed but left out of the rate.

## Job travelers

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/job-traveler-software

In the app today

## A job traveler from the quote you won

The estimate already holds the routing, so the floor's copy should not be typed again. Once a quote is won, the app prints a traveler per part from the quote's own operations, with no prices on it.

Start free

### What it does

- One sheet per part: customer, quote, PO and due date; quantity ordered and parts to start at the line's fallout
- The material, its stock description, the blank and the stock pieces or bars to pull, with a cut list for bar stock
- Every operation numbered 10, 20, 30 in the estimate's order with its work center, setup, cycle per part and run time
- Finishing and outside services after them, final inspection, a sign-off line per step and a heat/lot box
- The quantity from the PO you type, or the break the customer accepted online; a multi-break line with neither is refused, never guessed

### What it does not do yet

- A traveler is a PDF to print: there is no saved work order number, status or barcode time tracking yet
- Won quotes only

### Free guides on this

- How to quote a CNC machining job
- How to quote welding and fabrication jobs

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Do prices show on the traveler?

No. It carries quantities, material, operations and times only; no price, rate or markup appears on it.

## QuickBooks invoices from quotes

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/quickbooks-invoices-from-quotes

In the app today

## Invoice a won quote in QuickBooks without retyping it

The quote already says what the customer agreed to pay, so the bookkeeper should not key it in again. On a won quote, the app writes the invoice as a CSV in the shape QuickBooks Online's own invoice import takes.

Start free

### What it does

- One row per part at the quantity it was quoted at and that quantity's unit price and amount, the stored price exactly
- The quantity the customer accepted online, the only break, or the one you pick; a multi-break line with none of these is refused, never priced between breaks
- The invoice number Q1001 (Q1001-R2 for a revision), the customer, the invoice and due dates, and "Your PO ... Per our quote ..." as the message on the invoice
- The due date from "Net N" in your quote terms, else 30 days, changeable before download
- No costs, rates, markups or operations in the file: the same facts the customer's PDF prints

### What it does not do yet

- One won quote per file; there is no batch export of several quotes yet
- You upload the file in QuickBooks and match its columns there; the app does not know when it was imported
- QuickBooks Online does not take invoice imports in a company that has set up sales tax
- The one-click send to a connected QuickBooks company is built but not switched on in the hosted app yet

### Free guides on this

- Machine shop quote template
- How to quote a CNC machining job

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Does it work with QuickBooks Desktop?

The file is laid out for QuickBooks Online's invoice import. QuickBooks Desktop imports invoices differently, and the app does not write a Desktop file.

## Shop load and lead time

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/machine-shop-lead-time

In the app today

## Quote lead times from your real shop load

A lead time typed from habit ("3 weeks ARO") is the one promise a shop most often breaks. The Shop load page puts the open jobs on the machines, and a draft quote's card plans each quantity break behind them.

Start free

### What it does

- Open jobs (won and not shipped) placed on the machines by due date, each operation in the estimate's order at setup plus cycle times the starts
- Each machine's hours a day, Monday to Friday, set by an admin
- Each job's finish day and "after the due date" when it is late; each machine's open hours and the day it is booked until
- On a draft quote, "Lead time from shop load" gives the day, the working days and "N weeks ARO" for every quantity break
- A won quote's Job card saves the due date, the quantity ordered and the shipped day

### What it does not do yet

- Holidays, work already done on a job, finishing and outside-service days are not counted, and the page says so
- A machine with no hours a day or a line with no cycle time is listed as "can't plan" with the reason

### Free guides on this

- How to price a rush job
- How to work out a machine shop hourly rate
- How to quote outside processing (heat treat, plating)
- Machine shop quote template (free CSV)

### Common questions

### Which plans include it?

Every plan, including the free Early access plan (up to 40 RFQs a month, 3 people, no card). Plans differ by RFQs a month and seats, not by features. Paid plans start at $199 a month and are not on sale yet.

### Is this a full scheduling system?

No. It is a finite-capacity estimate from your quotes' own routings, good enough to quote a date. It does not track work done on the floor or move jobs around for you.

Yes. It opened in November 2026 and has no customers, reviews or published results yet. What this page describes works in the hosted app today; check every price, time and quantity before you send a quote.

## Privacy

Source: https://marisstella.app/jobshop/privacy

Privacy

## Site privacy notice

These pages have no forms and set no cookies, so they store nothing that identifies
you. Visits are counted by cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics.

### The app has its own policy

When you sign up, Job Shop Quote stores your account, your shop's rates, RFQs, files and quotes. What
it keeps, why and for how long is in its
privacy policy, alongside the
terms of service.

### Hosting

The site is served by Cloudflare, which, like any web host, sees the requests your browser
makes to it.

### Visit counts

Like the rest of marisstella.app, these pages load Cloudflare Web Analytics, which counts page
views, the page you came from and how fast pages load. It sets no cookies and keeps no identifier for
you, so the counts are aggregate. Blocking scripts from static.cloudflareinsights.com
stops it and the pages still work. The site's
privacy policy has the details.

### Earlier early-access requests

If you asked for early access through an earlier form and want your request deleted, email
hello@marisstella.app from the address you used.

### Who we are

Maris Stella Labs LLC.
